report.source_text: The patient commenced oncological treatment involving 28 fractions of radiotherapy (50.4 Gy to the pelvis and 56 Gy to a presacral node) and five cycles of once weekly Carboplatin. Subsequent brachytherapy was planned but abandoned due to difficult access to the uterus and so phase 2 external beam radiotherapy was given instead. On advice of rheumatology, the patient received 5 days of intravenous immunoglobins and a 4-week course of prednisolone 40 mg once daily. Methotrexate was also considered but given the patient was receiving platinum-based chemotherapy it was deemed of more risk than benefit to give two agents with immunosuppressive potential concurrently. The patient remained inpatient for a total of 59 days. During this time, she received multiple reviews from the speech and language team who cautiously assessed swallowing capabilities and amended feeding regimens accordingly to reduce risk of an aspiration pneumonia. As swallowing remained an issue for a number of weeks, dietetic involvement became crucial. The patient’s weight decreased dramatically following diagnosis and maintaining/gaining weight was imperative while receiving chemotherapy. A nasogastric tube was inserted for a short period to assist with this. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy input was invaluable; initially goals were to maintain muscle strength and avoid further muscle wasting in affected myotomes, then later build up muscle lost.

report.source_text: On review 1 month post-discharge, the patient had good movement in her arms and, although still very fatigued, was mobilising well. She returned to her usual diet with no swallowing difficulty and no evidence of cutaneous changes were found on examination. Prednisolone was continuing to be reduced. On further review 3 months post-discharge, steroids were now discontinued and symptoms continued to improve, so much so the patient was back to undertaking activities as per pre-diagnosis. Imaging with MRI and CT-PET showed a complete oncological response to treatment and so regular clinical surveillance continued via 3 monthly assessments.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Definite Dermatomyositis (DM) as a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with stage IIIC squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
clinician.trajectory_summary: A female in her 70s with stage IIIC SCC cervix (5 cm tumor, 3 cm internal iliac lymph node) presented with postmenopausal paravaginal bleeding and slowly progressive shoulder weakness. Three weeks after initiation of planned chemoradiotherapy, she presented acutely with dysphagia, severe proximal muscle myopathy (MRC 2/5 in shoulder abduction and hip flexion bilaterally), muscle wasting of shoulder girdles, hoarse voice, and slowed speech. Physical examination revealed a characteristic macular rash of purple/red discoloration over metacarpophalangeal joints, outer thighs, and knees bilaterally. Skin biopsy from the left thigh confirmed interface dermatitis with basal spongiosis, vacuolar degeneration, and mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Serological testing revealed positive anti-NXP2 antibodies (myositis-specific antibody strongly associated with cancer-associated myositis). Skeletal muscle enzymes were documented as raised. The clinical presentation of symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, characteristic cutaneous changes, raised skeletal muscle enzymes, and pathologically confirmed dermatitis established the diagnosis of definite dermatomyositis. The patient was treated with intravenous immunoglobulins and prednisolone 40 mg daily, along with multidisciplinary supportive care (speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy) during a 59-day admission. At 1 month post-discharge, she demonstrated good arm movement, returned to normal diet with resolution of dysphagia, and cutaneous changes had resolved. By 3 months post-discharge, steroids were discontinued and symptoms had substantially improved, with the patient returning to pre-diagnosis functional status. Imaging showed complete oncological response to cervical cancer treatment.
